title: H. G. Wells: The War of the Worlds — Ep 27/27 — "The Epilogue"
description:
The narrator closes his account with more doubts than answers. Carver's germs most likely killed the invaders, though only earthly bacteria were ever found in their bodies, and the Black Smoke and the Heat-Ray generator remain unexplained.

A graver question stays with him: each time Mars swings near, he expects the Martians to try again, and thinks we should watch that planet. Lessing believes they have already landed on Venus, and the narrator reflects that Earth is no safe, fenced home for Man — now every shooting star brings fear, and perhaps the defeat he witnessed is only a reprieve.

By lamplight he still sees the valley burning, the empty house behind him, carts and children fading like smoke on the Byfleet Road, and nights that bring back the black powder and the dead. In London the crowds of Fleet Street seem like ghosts to him, and on Primrose Hill, among the flower beds, he turns and reaches for his wife's hand, remembering the hill as it stood bright and hard and silent under the dawn of that last day.

That night his wife walks into his study, and each of them had counted the other among the dead. "I had counted you among the dead too, my dear, and here you are, warm," she tells him, as he holds her hand again.

Chapter X of Book Two of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds (1898), "The Epilogue", in the public domain.

— The Keeper's Lantern —
Every episode is one whole chapter, in order, from the first page to the last.
